Sequential AIPE Check for the Squared Multiple Correlation Coefficient

Source: R/seq_aipe_R2.R
seq_aipe_R2.Rd

Given the predictors and the response collected so far, evaluates whether the sequential accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE) stopping rule of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2019) has been satisfied for the population squared multiple correlation coefficient, and returns the current estimate with its confidence interval. Use it when the goal is a confidence interval for the population squared multiple correlation that is no wider than a chosen width and the population value needed to plan a fixed sample size is unknown.

Usage

seq_aipe_R2(
  x,
  y,
  width,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  ci_method = c("wald", "log_transformed")
)

Arguments

x

The predictors collected so far: a numeric matrix or a data frame of numeric columns with one row per observation and one column per predictor, or a numeric vector for a single predictor. Do not include a column of ones; the intercept is part of the model.

y

Numeric vector. The response collected so far, one value per row of x.

width

The target full width of the confidence interval for the population squared multiple correlation coefficient (\(\omega\) in the article). A single number greater than 0 and less than 1.

conf_level

The confidence level (default 0.95). A single number strictly between 0 and 1.

ci_method

Which confidence interval to report and to build the stopping rule on: "wald" (the default; the symmetric interval with the Olkin and Finn, 1995, variance) or "log_transformed" (the Bonett and Wright, 2011, interval).

Value

An object of class c("smsd_check", "data.frame") with columns term and value and six rows:

lower_limit

The lower confidence limit.

R2

The sample squared multiple correlation coefficient.

upper_limit

The upper confidence limit.

xi_squared

The estimated asymptotic variance of \(R^2\) under multivariate normality, \(4 R^2 (1 - R^2)^2\) (Olkin and Finn, 1995). The Wald standard error is its square root over \(\sqrt{n}\). It is reported as computed; no lower bound is applied to it.

criterion_n

The criterion sample size of the stopping rule, given the current data. The rule is met when current_n is at least this number. When no decision can be made it is at least current_n + 1.

current_n

The number of observations supplied.

A quantity that is not defined for the current data is NA: the two limits whenever no decision can be made (the variance estimate is unusable, the estimate cannot be computed, or ci_method = "log_transformed" and \(n = p + 2\)), and R2 and xi_squared when the response does not vary. The attributes are:

method

The label of the method, which names the interval: "squared multiple correlation, Wald interval" or "squared multiple correlation, log transformed interval".

is_satisfied

TRUE when the stopping rule is met, otherwise FALSE; never NA. It is TRUE exactly when current_n is at least criterion_n.

current_n, criterion_n

The two sample sizes, as integers.

conf_level, width

As supplied.

notes

A character vector, of length zero when there is nothing to say, that print() shows under the stopping line. The notes that say why no decision can be made (the estimate cannot be computed; the variance estimate is unusable; the log transformed interval is not yet defined) accompany a rule that is not met. The note that the sample is small relative to the number of predictors can accompany either decision and does not change it.

ci_method

The interval used, "wald" or "log_transformed".

p

The number of predictors.

variance_unusable

TRUE when the variance estimate is unusable (zero, or not finite because the estimate cannot be computed), otherwise FALSE.

Details

This procedure assumes multivariate normality. Unlike the correlation procedures of the same article (seq_aipe_r) and the other seq_aipe_* functions, it is not distribution free: the article develops it for multivariate normal data only (p. 503), because no distribution free interval for the squared multiple correlation was available. See the section on assumptions below.

The coverage guarantee is asymptotic and can fail badly in small samples, above all with many predictors. Coverage approaches the confidence level as the target width narrows and the sample grows for interior population values, \(0 < \mathrm{P}^2 < 1\), under the stated assumptions. At the null boundary \(\mathrm{P}^2 = 0\), the normal approximation is degenerate; increasing the sample size does not restore the usual Wald calibration. See the section on the null boundary. At a wide target it falls short even with few predictors: with five predictors, a 95% level, and a target width of .30 it was .851 for a population value of .50 and .797 for a population value of .90. It falls much further when the number of predictors is not small relative to the sample size that the width calls for. The sample \(R^2\) overestimates the population value by roughly \((1 - \mathrm{P}^2) p / n\), both intervals are built around it, and the stopping rule does not correct for it, so the rule is met with an interval that tends to lie above the population value. In simulations of the full procedure with multivariate normal data and a 95% level (10,000 replications per condition), coverage with the default interval for a population value of .50 was .865 with 10 predictors and .790 with 15 at a target width of .20, and .668 with 10 and .361 with 15 at a target width of .30. With 20 predictors unrelated to the response (a population value of 0) and a target width of .30, the final interval contained 0 in 4% of replications; in 36% of data sets the rule was met at the very first check, with 27 observations, a sample value near .88, and a lower limit near .80. The article offers no remedy, and the function does not alter the stopping rule to correct for it. What it does is say so: whenever an interval is reported from a sample that is small relative to the number of predictors (fewer than \(p \max(20, 2p)\) observations), the object returned carries a note (see the section on small samples below). The article's own simulations cover 2, 5, and 10 predictors at widths of .05 and .10. Before relying on the procedure, run seq_aipe_R2_sensitivity at the planned width and number of predictors; a larger pilot sample (m_0 in seq_aipe_R2_pilot) helps. See the sections on the asymptotic guarantee and on small samples below.

The function is stateless. After collecting the pilot sample, whose size seq_aipe_R2_pilot gives, the user calls seq_aipe_R2() and, while the rule is not met, adds observations and calls it again on all the data collected so far.

seq_path applies the function to data already in hand at every sample size from the pilot sample size on. For most procedures it works out the pilot sample size itself. For this one it cannot, because the pilot sample size depends on the number of predictors, which the check function reads from the data and seq_path() has no way to hand to the pilot function; called without start it stops with a message. Supply the start, as in the last example:

seq_path(seq_aipe_R2, list(x = x, y = y), width = width,
         start = seq_aipe_R2_pilot(width, p = ncol(x)))

The printed path gives the stopping point and the interval there but not the notes of the check at that point, so a path that stops while the sample is small relative to the number of predictors (see the section on small samples below) prints without that note. The check at the stopping point, with its notes, is attr(path, "final_check"); look at it before the interval is reported.

Estimator and Confidence Intervals

With \(n\) observations on \(p\) predictors (\(k\) in the article) and a response, the estimate is the sample squared multiple correlation coefficient \(R^2\) (Equation 57 of the article), the value summary(lm(y ~ x))$r.squared reports. Write \(R\) for its positive square root, \(\omega\) for width, and \(z = z_{1-\alpha/2}\) for the standard normal quantile.

The article studies two intervals, both with \(R\) in place of the population value in the standard error:

  • ci_method = "wald" (Equation 59), built on the asymptotic variance \(4 \mathrm{P}^2 (1 - \mathrm{P}^2)^2 / n\) of Olkin and Finn (1995, p. 161, Equation 10): $$R^2 \pm z \, \frac{2 R (1 - R^2)}{\sqrt{n}}.$$

  • ci_method = "log_transformed" (Equation 58), the interval of Bonett and Wright (2011), formed for \(\ln(1 - R^2)\) and transformed back: $$1 - \exp\left\{\ln(1 - R^2) \pm z \, \frac{2 R}{\sqrt{n - p - 2}}\right\}.$$

Neither interval is truncated to \([0, 1]\) in the article, and the limits are returned as computed: with either interval the lower limit can be negative, and with the Wald interval the upper limit can exceed 1 when the sample is very small (\(n < 4 z^2 R^2\)). Once the stopping rule is met the interval is no wider than \(\omega\). The log transformed interval is not defined at \(n = p + 2\), where its limits are returned as NA.

The Wald interval is the default because the article concludes from its simulations (p. 506) that the procedure built on it did better than the one built on the log transformed interval in terms of the sample size required; its coverage is also closer to the confidence level in 59 of the 60 conditions of the article's Tables 11 to 14 (see the section on the asymptotic guarantee).

Stopping Rule

The rule is met when \(n\) is at least criterion_n, the smallest whole number not below

  • for "wald": $$\frac{16 z^2}{\omega^2} \left(R^2 + \frac{1}{n}\right) \left(1 - R^2 + \frac{1}{n}\right)^2;$$

  • for "log_transformed" (Equation 62): $$p + 2 + \frac{4 R^2 z^2}{L^2}, \quad L = \ln\left[\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\omega}{1 - R^2} + \sqrt{\frac{\omega^2}{(1 - R^2)^2} + 4}\right)\right].$$

These estimate the sample sizes that would be needed if the population value \(\mathrm{P}^2\) were known (Equations 61 and 60): \(16 z^2 \mathrm{P}^2 (1 - \mathrm{P}^2)^2 / \omega^2\) for the Wald interval, and the log transformed expression with \(\mathrm{P}^2\) in place of \(R^2\). The terms \(1/n\) in the Wald rule are the correction that keeps sampling from stopping too early; the log transformed rule has no such correction in the article.

The Wald rule differs from Equation 63 as printed. The printed equation has \((1 - (R^2 + 1/n))^2\) as its last factor, which lowers the criterion whenever \(R^2\) is above about one third, allows the interval at the stopping point to be wider than \(\omega\), and does not reproduce the article's Tables 13 and 14. In simulations of all 60 conditions of those tables the printed form gave a mean final sample size below the tabled value in every condition, by more than three standard errors in 49 of them (and by as much as 39.7), and a mean interval width above \(\omega\) in 27. The form above, with both factors increased by \(1/n\), reproduced all 60 conditions within Monte Carlo error; it never lowers the criterion, and it guarantees a width of at most \(\omega\) at the stopping point. The package implements the form that reproduces the published results.

When no decision can be made the rule is "not met". As in the other seq_aipe_* check functions, when the variance estimate is unusable or the estimate cannot be computed, the rule is reported as not met, the limits are NA, criterion_n is at least one more than current_n, the attribute variance_unusable is TRUE, and a note says why (see smsd_check_methods). This is a deliberate departure from the rules as printed, which would be met at once with an interval of zero width.

For this procedure the variance estimate, \(4 R^2 (1 - R^2)^2\), is unusable when the sample \(R^2\) is 0 or 1 to within the precision of the data (for example because the response is an exact linear function of the predictors), which makes the estimate zero, and it cannot be computed when the response does not vary. A positive estimate, however small, is used as it stands: the lower bound of \(n^{-3}\) that the distribution free procedures in this package place on their variance estimates is not part of this procedure. The rule is also reported as not met, with limits of NA and a note, while the log transformed interval is not yet defined (\(n = p + 2\)).

A variable whose values agree to ten significant digits counts as not varying, as everywhere in this package: such a predictor is an error, and such a response is the case in which the estimate cannot be computed. Whether \(R^2\) is 0 or 1 is likewise judged to the precision of the data. For ordinary data that is the precision of the arithmetic. When a variable is a large constant plus a small spread (a mean more than about 700,000 times the standard deviation, as with long identifiers or time stamps), the last digits of its stored values are rounding error, and a share of the sum of squares small enough to be that error alone is treated as zero. Subtracting a constant from such a variable before calling avoids both and does not change \(R^2\).

Assumptions

The predictors and the response are assumed to be independent draws from a multivariate normal distribution (so the predictors are random, not fixed by design). Both standard errors come from the normal theory variance of \(R^2\), which is too small for heavy tailed data, so the intervals are then too narrow however large the sample. In simulations of the full procedure with three predictors, a population value of .50, a target width of .10, and a 95% level (40,000 replications per condition), coverage with the Wald interval was .946 for multivariate normal data, .902 for a multivariate t distribution with 10 degrees of freedom, .788 for a multivariate t distribution with 5 degrees of freedom, and .860 when the predictors and the error were independent right skewed variables (standardized chi square with 3 degrees of freedom). A narrower target does not help: at a width of .05 coverage was .948 for normal data and .782 for the t distribution with 5 degrees of freedom. The log transformed interval behaved the same way (.938, .896, .773, and .851 at a width of .10). The article offers no remedy, and this function should not be used for data that are far from multivariate normal.

The Null Boundary

When all \(p\) predictors and the response are independent normal variables and the population squared multiple correlation is zero, the fixed sample distribution is \(R^2 \sim \mathrm{Beta}(p/2, (n-p-1)/2)\). In particular, \(n R^2\) approaches a chi squared distribution with \(p\) degrees of freedom, rather than the normal approximation with positive variance used by the Wald interval. Its lower limit includes zero only when \(n R^2 \leq 4 z^2 (1-R^2)^2\). Its limiting fixed sample coverage is therefore \(\Pr(\chi^2_p \leq 4 z^2)\), which is about 24.49% for \(p=20\) and a nominal 95% level. This is a fixed sample limit, not the coverage of the sequential stopping rule. It shows why a larger pilot alone cannot establish nominal coverage at the null boundary. Moreover, when \(p=20\), no legal fixed sample size gives 95% coverage with this Wald interval. Put \(c=4z^2\). The inclusion event implies \(R^2 \leq c/n\). The beta distribution's mean and variance, together with a one sided variance inequality, bound its probability by \(40/(40+(20-c)^2)\), or about 65.07%, for every \(n>21\). This loose bound rules out 95% coverage at any fixed sample size; the limit above gives the sharper large sample result.

Asymptotic Guarantee

For fixed \(p\) and an interior population value \(0 < \mathrm{P}^2 < 1\), the coverage of the interval at the stopping point approaches the confidence level as the target width narrows; it is not guaranteed at any particular width, and the article notes (p. 508) that the procedure works well as the sample size increases but not for small sample sizes. With five predictors, multivariate normal data, and a 95% level (10,000 replications per condition), coverage with the Wald interval for a population value of .50 was .851 at a target width of .30, .912 at .20, .936 at .10, and .949 at .05; with the log transformed interval it was .831, .896, .930, and .939. Among these interior conditions, Wald coverage is lowest when the population value is large: for .90 it was .797 at a width of .30, .848 at .20, .901 at .10, and .913 at .05. The log transformed interval, which can stop within a few observations of its pilot sample size, does not improve steadily as the target narrows: for a population value of .90 it gave .925, .906, .774, and .847 at the same four widths. The article's Tables 11 to 14 show the same pattern at widths of .05 and .10: at the 95% level its coverage ranges from .830 to .954 for the Wald interval and from .646 to .949 for the log transformed interval.

Coverage also falls, much further, when the sample is small relative to the number of predictors; see the next section. (The Monte Carlo standard error of each coverage from a simulation of the full procedure reported on this page for a single condition is at most .011, and at most .005 where 10,000 replications are stated; a condition that appears in two places comes from two separate runs.)

Small Samples Relative to the Number of Predictors

The sample \(R^2\) overestimates the population value by roughly \((1 - \mathrm{P}^2) p / n\). In standard errors that is about \(p / (2 \mathrm{P} \sqrt{n})\), and both intervals are built around the sample value. Their coverage is therefore below the confidence level until \(n\) is large relative to \(p\) and, with many predictors, relative to \(p^2\). Olkin and Finn (1995, p. 161) give their variance as an approximation for samples in which, in the notation used here, \(2p + 5\) is small relative to \(n\). The stopping rule takes no account of this: with a wide target or many predictors it can be met at the pilot sample size.

The note. Whenever an interval is reported from fewer than \(p \max(20, 2p)\) observations, the object returned carries a note that says so. That is fewer than 20 observations per predictor or, with more than 10 predictors, fewer than \(2p\) per predictor: 40 observations with 2 predictors, 100 with 5, 200 with 10, 800 with 20. The note depends on \(n\) and \(p\) alone. It does not change is_satisfied: the article has no remedy for the shortfall, and none is invented here. It marks the sample sizes at which the interval should not be relied on without checking the design with seq_aipe_R2_sensitivity.

The threshold is where the coverage of the Wald interval at a fixed sample size and a 95% level reaches about .90 for population values of .30 or more. With 2 to 40 predictors and population values of .30, .50, .70, and .90 (400,000 samples per condition from the exact distribution of \(R^2\) under multivariate normality, which Gatsonis and Sampson, 1989, p. 517, give), that coverage was between .902 and .928 at exactly \(p \max(20, 2p)\) observations, between .847 and .904 at half as many, and between .714 and .855 at a quarter as many; at twice as many it was between .927 and .938. (With one predictor it was between .864 and .891 at 20 observations. At the 90% and 99% levels it was between .834 and .870 and between .953 and .981 at the threshold.) A smaller population value needs a larger sample: for a population value of .10 the coverage at the threshold was between .834 and .934. The log transformed interval does better at a fixed sample size (between .912 and .950 at the threshold and between .799 and .957 at a quarter of it), but the sequential procedure built on it stops earlier.

In simulations of the full sequential procedure at a 95% level (population values of .10, .30, .50, .70, and .90; 500 to 2,000 replications per condition; every condition given the same weight), coverage among the replications that stopped with the note depended above all on the number of predictors. With the Wald interval it was .793 with 2 predictors, .817 with 5, .663 with 10, .428 with 20, and .180 with 30. Among the replications that stopped without the note it was .915 with 1 predictor (with which the note was never attached), .933 with 2, .942 with 5, .917 with 10, .927 with 20, and .892 with 30. With the log transformed interval coverage with the note was .466, .732, .807, .755, .615, and .422 with 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, and 30 predictors, and without it between .923 and .951. The conditions are not fully crossed: the target widths were .05, .07, .10, .15, .20, .30, and .40 with 1, 2, and 5 predictors, .10 to .40 with 10 predictors, .07 to .40 with 20, and .05, .20, and .30 with 30 (175 conditions for each interval). A single figure for all replications that stopped with the note therefore depends on which conditions are pooled, and none is offered: for the Wald interval it is .530 over all 175 conditions, .811 over those with 1, 2, and 5 predictors, and .439 over those with widths of .20 and .30, which every number of predictors has. The figure without the note depends on that far less (.926, .928, and .914).

By the sample size at the stopping point relative to the threshold, for population values of .30 or more and over all of those conditions, coverage with the Wald interval was .780 from a quarter to a half of the threshold, .877 from a half to the threshold, .901 from the threshold to twice it, .928 from twice to four times it, and .949 beyond; with the log transformed interval it was .815, .911, .938, .946, and .951. Below a quarter of the threshold it again depended on the number of predictors: .601 with 5, .395 with 10, .243 with 20, and .115 with 30 for the Wald interval (with 1 and 2 predictors no replication stopped there), and .239, .587, .643, .607, .506, and .399 with 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, and 30 for the log transformed interval.

The note is a statement about \(n\) and \(p\) and nothing else, so it is neither a verdict nor a guarantee. Coverage can be at the confidence level with it: with five predictors, a population value of .10, and a width of .30, 90% of replications stopped with the note and coverage was .941. And coverage can be below the confidence level without it, for the reasons given in the previous section: at a wide target and for a small population value. Among the replications with 1, 2, and 5 predictors that stopped without the note, Wald coverage for a population value of .50 was .949 at a width of .10 and .918 at .30, and for a population value of .10 it was between .864 and .942 across the seven widths. With a single predictor, for which the pilot sample size at these widths is 20 or more, so that the note is never attached, coverage for a population value of .10 was between .80 and .89 at widths of .10 to .40.

Some single conditions, each from a run of its own. For a population value of .50 at the 95% level (10,000 replications per condition; 4,000 for 40 predictors at a width of .10), coverage with the Wald interval at a target width of .30 was .900 with 2 predictors, .845 with 5, .668 with 10, .361 with 15, .071 with 20, and 0 with 40 (where every replication stopped at the pilot sample size of 42); at a width of .20 it was .865 with 10 predictors and .790 with 15; at a width of .10 it was .948, .942, .934, .903, and .778 with 2, 5, 10, 20, and 40. The log transformed interval gave .885, .837, .709, .563, .427, and .076 at a width of .30, .829 and .748 at .20, and .936, .926, .906, .851, and .671 at .10. When the predictors are unrelated to the response (a population value of 0), coverage at a width of .30 was .971 with 5 predictors, .711 with 10, and .040 with 20 for the Wald interval, and .967, .847, and .273 for the log transformed interval. This case does not improve with the sample size, because the variance \(4 \mathrm{P}^2 (1 - \mathrm{P}^2)^2\) on which both intervals rest is zero there: the Wald interval contains 0 when \(n R^2 \le 4 z^2 (1 - R^2)^2\), so as \(n\) grows its coverage tends to the probability that a chi square variable with \(p\) degrees of freedom is at most \(4 z^2\), which at the 95% level is .991, .881, .575, and .245 for 5, 10, 15, and 20 predictors (at a fixed sample size of 400 observations per predictor, 100,000 samples each: .990, .877, .569, and .240).

A larger pilot sample. The one thing in the user's hands is m_0 in seq_aipe_R2_pilot. With 20 predictors, a population value of .50, and a width of .30, pilot samples of 100, 200, and 400 gave coverage of .601, .789, and .877 with the Wald interval. With the pilot sample size at the threshold itself, m_0 = p * max(20, 2 * p), so that no interval is ever reported with the note, coverage with the Wald interval was between .896 and .932 for 5, 10, and 20 predictors, population values of .30 to .90, and widths of .20 and .30 (2,000 replications per condition), where the default pilot sample size gave between .019 and .932; for a population value of .10 it was between .853 and .953. The log transformed interval gave between .920 and .955 (default pilot sample size: .373 to .930), and between .875 and .966 for a population value of .10. The price is the sample size: with 20 predictors, a population value of .50, and a width of .30 that pilot sample is 800 observations, where the rule by itself stops near 33. This is not part of the article's procedure and is not a default; the article's own simulations cover 2, 5, and 10 predictors at widths of .05 and .10. Use seq_aipe_R2_sensitivity to see what to expect at the width, number of predictors, and pilot sample size of a planned study before relying on the procedure.

References

Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2019). Sequential accuracy in parameter estimation for population correlation coefficients. Psychological Methods, 24(4), 492–515. doi:10.1037/met0000203

Kelley, K. (2008). Sample size planning for the squared multiple correlation coefficient: Accuracy in parameter estimation via narrow confidence intervals. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 43(4), 524–555. doi:10.1080/00273170802490632

Bonett, D. G., & Wright, T. A. (2011). Sample size requirements for multiple regression interval estimation. Journal of Organizational Behavior, 32(6), 822–830. doi:10.1002/job.717

Gatsonis, C., & Sampson, A. R. (1989). Multiple correlation: Exact power and sample size calculations. Psychological Bulletin, 106(3), 516–524.

Olkin, I., & Finn, J. D. (1995). Correlations redux. Psychological Bulletin, 118(1), 155–164. doi:10.1037/0033-2909.118.1.155

See also

seq_aipe_R2_pilot, seq_aipe_R2_sensitivity; seq_path for the whole stopping path of data in hand; smsd_check_methods for the methods of the returned object; seq_aipe_r for the distribution free procedures for a single correlation; in DMAR, the fixed sample size planner ss_aipe_R2 and the confidence interval ci_R2 (Kelley, 2008), which invert the exact sampling distribution of \(R^2\) rather than use an approximate standard error.

Other seq_aipe_R2: seq_aipe_R2_pilot(), seq_aipe_R2_sensitivity()

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu, Francis Bilson Darku fbilsond@nd.edu, Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in

Examples

# How well do autonomy, supervisor support, and workload together predict
# job satisfaction? The goal is a 95% confidence interval for the
# population squared multiple correlation no wider than 0.25.
set.seed(113)
survey <- function(n) {
  predictors <- cbind(autonomy = rnorm(n), support = rnorm(n),
                      workload = rnorm(n))
  satisfaction <- drop(predictors %*% c(0.45, 0.40, -0.30)) + rnorm(n)
  list(x = predictors, y = satisfaction)
}
m <- seq_aipe_R2_pilot(width = 0.25, p = 3)
employees <- survey(m)
out <- seq_aipe_R2(employees$x, employees$y, width = 0.25)
# Not met, with a note: 32 observations are few for three predictors.
out
#> Sequential check (squared multiple correlation, Wald interval)
#> 
#>   Current n       : 32
#>   Criterion n     : 104
#>   Target width    : 0.25
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : 0.42985
#>   R2                : 0.6324142
#>   upper_limit       : 0.8349784
#>   xi_squared        : 0.3418055
#>   criterion_n       : 104
#>   current_n         : 32
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE
#> 
#>   Note: With 32 observations and 3 predictors the sample is small
#>         relative to the number of predictors (fewer than 60
#>         observations, 20 per predictor). The sample squared multiple
#>         correlation then overestimates the population value, and in
#>         simulations the interval of this procedure contained the
#>         population value less often than the confidence level, far less
#>         often the smaller the sample. This note does not change the
#>         stopping rule. See 'Small Samples Relative to the Number of
#>         Predictors' in the help of seq_aipe_R2().

# Survey ten more employees at a time until the stopping rule is met.
while (!attr(out, "is_satisfied")) {
  more <- survey(10)
  employees <- list(x = rbind(employees$x, more$x),
                    y = c(employees$y, more$y))
  out <- seq_aipe_R2(employees$x, employees$y, width = 0.25)
}
out
#> Sequential check (squared multiple correlation, Wald interval)
#> 
#>   Current n       : 152
#>   Criterion n     : 149
#>   Target width    : 0.25
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : 0.2709712
#>   R2                : 0.3920038
#>   upper_limit       : 0.5130364
#>   xi_squared        : 0.5796315
#>   criterion_n       : 149
#>   current_n         : 152
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: TRUE

# The same data one employee at a time, as a path. seq_path() cannot work
# out the pilot sample size for this procedure (it depends on the number
# of predictors), so the start is supplied.
path <- seq_path(seq_aipe_R2, employees, width = 0.25,
                 start = seq_aipe_R2_pilot(width = 0.25, p = 3))
attr(path, "stop_n")
#> [1] 149
# The check at the stopping point. Its notes, if it has any, are shown
# here and not when the path itself is printed.
attr(path, "final_check")
